question: In order for Mateen to walk a kilometer (\(1000\) meters) in his rectangular backyard, he must walk the length \(25\) times or walk its perimeter \(10\) times. What is the area of Mateen’s backyard in square meters?
solution:
Walking the length \(25\) times covers \(1000\) meters, so one length is
\[
1000\div25=40\text{ meters}.
\]
Similarly, walking the perimeter \(10\) times covers \(1000\) meters, so the perimeter is \(1000\div10=100\) meters.

A rectangle has two equal lengths and two equal widths. The two lengths account for \(2\cdot40=80\) meters of the perimeter, leaving \(100-80=20\) meters for the two widths. Each width is therefore \(20\div2=10\) meters.

The area is length times width:
\[
40\cdot10=\boxed{400}\text{ square meters},
\]
choice C.

edges.reason: Describing rectangle and square properties presupposes recognizing which plane shapes those names designate.

Written columns support perimeter arithmetic with larger dimensions. Adding decomposed lengths mentally gives the same result even for two-digit sides, so Gemini's chosen calculation does not establish column-method necessity.
The perimeter formulas use rectangle opposite-side equality and square side equality to combine their boundary lengths.
The target explicitly distinguishes boundary length from area. Perimeter meaning is required for that contrast, not all rectangle/square perimeter computations.
Two-digit columns support larger numerical areas. Repeated unit-square counts or decomposed multiplication can also compute an area, so no fixed dimension range is imposed by this preparation link.
